messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Data Scientist
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 40

# The Weight of Small Hands

Marco is twenty-five years old, a data scientist at a mid-sized tech firm in Austin, and the kind of person who has always found comfort in numbers. Patterns make sense to him. Probabilities feel like solid ground. What happened three years ago with his younger sister, Valentina, shook that ground in ways he is still trying to understand.

Valentina was seven when she was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Marco was twenty-two, the oldest of four children, and the one their mother leaned on most heavily when their father was working double shifts. He remembers the afternoon the diagnosis came clearly — the fluorescent lights of the pediatric oncology ward, the way the doctor's voice seemed to arrive from somewhere far away, and Valentina sitting on the examination table swinging her small legs, not yet understanding what any of it meant. Marco understood enough for both of them.

For the next fourteen months, he drove his mother to the hospital three times a week, sat in waiting rooms with his laptop open, and tried to keep working while Valentina moved in and out of crises that the medical team described in statistics he knew how to read but wished he didn't. There were two nights when the family was told to prepare themselves. He held his mother both times. He did not cry until he was alone in his car.

Valentina survived. She is now ten, healthy, back in school, obsessed with soccer. Everyone in the family speaks of her recovery as a miracle, a closed chapter, a reason to be grateful. Marco agrees with all of this and means it. But something in him did not close when the chapter did.

He notices it most at night. Sleep comes reluctantly and leaves early, interrupted by dreams that don't always feature Valentina directly but carry the same feeling — the sensation of waiting for something terrible, of being responsible for preventing something he cannot control. He wakes with his heart already racing, lying still in the dark of his apartment, running through a kind of internal checklist until his body believes it is safe.

At work, he is good at what he does, but concentration has become effortful in a way it never used to be. He finds himself reading the same block of code three times, his mind drifting back to a particular image — Valentina's hand bruised from an IV line, her hair gone, her eyes still trusting him completely. He has built small rituals to manage these moments: a specific playlist, a particular brand of coffee, a desk organized just so. His colleagues find him a little rigid. He doesn't explain.

He has pulled back from the family somewhat, which confuses him and produces guilt he carries quietly. Visits to his mother's house, which now include a laughing, healthy Valentina, sometimes trigger a tightness in his chest he cannot entirely explain. He loves her. Seeing her well should feel like relief, and it does, but underneath the relief there is something else — a residue of all those months of dread that his nervous system does not seem to know is over.

He has not been in a relationship since before Valentina's diagnosis. He tells himself he has been busy, which is partly true. But he also notices that closeness feels risky in a way it didn't before, as though loving someone creates a vulnerability he is no longer sure he can afford.

He came to therapy after a colleague mentioned offhandedly that Marco seemed "somewhere else" lately. The observation landed harder than it should have. He sat with it for two weeks before making the call. In his first session, he described himself as fine, then paused, then said — almost to himself — that he thought he might still be in that waiting room. That he wasn't sure he had ever really left.
